title: Servant Leadership Accelerator
blurb: Six weeks to lead with clarity and service — anchored in your Team21 360° assessment, the Leadership Growth Journey, the 3Ps, and a mentor-reviewed Personal Growth Plan.

modules.d: Serve first, lead second — the roots, the research, and what it looks like on a Monday morning.
modules.body:
A different starting question

Most leadership models begin with the question "How do I get people to do what needs doing?" Servant leadership begins somewhere else: "What do the people I lead need in order to grow, and to accomplish something worth accomplishing?" Robert Greenleaf, who coined the term in his 1970 essay The Servant as Leader, put the test plainly: do those served grow as persons — do they become healthier, wiser, freer, more autonomous, and more likely themselves to become servants? A leader who hits every target while leaving people diminished has failed Greenleaf's test.

This is not softness. Servant leaders set high standards, make hard decisions and hold people accountable. The difference is motive and direction: authority is used for the mission and the people, not for the leader's status, comfort or image. That distinction becomes visible under pressure — in who gets credit, who absorbs blame, and whose needs are considered when resources are scarce.

"Not so with you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant." — Matthew 20:26. Jesus spoke these words to disciples arguing over rank, and then washed their feet (John 13). The servant-leadership tradition Team21 teaches is rooted here: greatness is redefined, not abolished.

The characteristics, translated into behaviour

Larry Spears, drawing on Greenleaf's writing, described ten characteristics. They are most useful as observable behaviours, not virtues to admire:

  • Listening — you speak last in meetings where your opinion would end discussion.
  • Empathy — you assume good intent and seek to understand before correcting.
  • Healing — you repair trust after conflict instead of letting it fester.
  • Awareness — you know your own patterns, triggers and impact on others.
  • Persuasion — you build agreement rather than relying on positional power.
  • Conceptualisation — you hold the long-range vision while managing the day.
  • Foresight — you learn from the past to anticipate consequences.
  • Stewardship — you treat the organisation, its resources and its people as held in trust.
  • Commitment to the growth of people — you invest in development even when it costs you short-term output.
  • Building community — you create belonging, not just a reporting line.

What the research says — and does not say

Servant leadership has moved from philosophy into serious empirical study. Validated measures (for example, Liden and colleagues' servant-leadership scale) allow comparison with other styles. Across many studies, servant leadership is associated with higher employee engagement, trust, organisational citizenship behaviour, team performance and lower turnover intention, and meta-analytic work suggests it explains outcomes beyond what transformational leadership alone explains. Honest leaders should also note the limits: most studies are correlational, effects vary by culture and context, and "servant" behaviour can be faked for image. The research supports the practice; it does not make it automatic.

Servant leadership versus its imitations

Three distortions are common. The pleaser avoids conflict and calls it kindness — but withholding honest feedback denies people growth. The martyr does everyone's work and calls it service — but this creates dependency and exhaustion. The performer uses humble language publicly while controlling privately. Genuine servant leadership is recognisable by its fruit: people around the leader become more capable, more honest, and more able to lead themselves.

Since 2016, Team21 has taught this across three continents. The consistent lesson from that work: servant leadership scales best where resources are thinnest, because it multiplies the capability of the people you already have instead of waiting for resources you do not.

Why it matters more in the AI era

As machines take over more routine analysis and production, the work that remains distinctly human — judgement, trust, care, meaning, moral courage — becomes the core of leadership. John Lennox, in 2084, observes that the deepest questions AI raises are not technical but human: identity, purpose, worth. Servant leadership answers from conviction that people are ends, never merely means. That conviction becomes more valuable every year the technology improves.

Your pre-work

Before Week 2, write short answers to the identity questions: What are your passions? What long-term aspirations do you hold? What legacy do you want to leave? Which communities do you want to influence? Then launch your Team21 360° assessment with at least six raters across levels — manager, peers, direct reports and someone outside work.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Begin my Team21 Leadership Growth Journey. You are my Leadership Growth AI Mentor. Ask me one question at a time about my passions, long-term aspirations, the legacy I want, and the communities I want to influence. After my answers, reflect back the themes you notice and ask one challenging question about where my current leadership behaviour does or does not match those answers.

📚 Glossary

  • Servant leadership: leading by prioritising the growth of people and the good of the mission over the leader's status
  • Greenleaf's test: whether those served grow as persons and become servants themselves
  • Stewardship: holding people and resources in trust for a purpose larger than yourself
  • Organisational citizenship behaviour: voluntary effort that helps colleagues and the organisation beyond formal duties

📖 References

  • Greenleaf, R. K. (1970). The Servant as Leader.
  • Spears, L. (2010). Character and servant leadership. Journal of Virtues & Leadership.
  • Liden, R. et al. (2008). Servant leadership: development of a multidimensional measure. Leadership Quarterly.
  • Hoch, J. et al. (2018). Do ethical, authentic, and servant leadership explain variance above transformational leadership? Journal of Management.
  • Lennox, J. (2020). 2084: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Humanity.

quiz.q: Grace runs a microfinance branch in Bamenda that has beaten its loan targets three years running, yet two of her best loan officers resigned this year saying they had learned nothing new since joining. Applying Greenleaf's test, how should her leadership be judged?
opts: Falling short just if the departures start pulling the branch below target
Falling short, since the people she leads are not growing and are leaving
Sound, provided exit interviews show the resignations were for personal reasons
Sound overall, since sustained results show staff are being served well enough
quiz.x: Greenleaf's test asks whether those served grow as persons. Targets met while capable people stagnate and leave fail it. The exit-interview option is the runner-up but still judges by results, not growth.

quiz.q: Marie, a hospital nursing supervisor in Douala, stays until 11 pm most nights rewriting her nurses' shift handover notes herself rather than returning them, saying she is protecting the team from criticism. Which distortion does this most closely match?
opts: The martyr, because doing their work creates dependency and exhausts her
The pleaser, because she is avoiding the discomfort of an honest conversation
The performer, because she wants the ward to look good to senior management
Healthy stewardship, because she is guarding the quality of patient records
quiz.x: Doing others' work and calling it service is the martyr pattern: dependency plus exhaustion. The pleaser is the runner-up (she also avoids feedback), but the defining behaviour here is taking over the work.

quiz.q: Daniel, CEO of a 200-person logistics firm in Texas, notices that whenever he states his preference early in a strategy session, debate stops and everyone agrees. Which practice best reflects servant-leadership listening?
opts: Send his view in writing beforehand so the meeting can focus on execution
Open by stating his view clearly so the team can challenge it from the start
Speak last, after asking each person for their view and probing the options
Stay silent throughout and let the team reach a decision without his input
quiz.x: The lesson defines listening as speaking last where your opinion would end discussion. Staying silent entirely is the runner-up but withholds a leader's needed contribution and judgement.

quiz.q: A team lead at a Yaounde consultancy has not told Paul that his monthly reports contain recurring errors, explaining that servant leaders are kind and supportive. How should this be evaluated?
opts: It reflects empathy, which should come before correction in the Spears list
It is acceptable as long as the team lead quietly corrects the reports herself
It is a reasonable short-term choice that protects Paul's confidence and trust
It is the pleaser distortion: withholding honest feedback denies Paul growth
quiz.x: Servant leaders hold high standards; avoiding conflict and calling it kindness is the pleaser. Quietly correcting the reports adds the martyr pattern, and empathy means understanding before correcting, not instead of it.

quiz.q: A board member at a Nairobi NGO argues that research proves servant leadership will raise any team's performance, so the board should mandate it. Which response is most defensible given the evidence?
opts: Disagree: the evidence is mainly anecdotal and lacks validated measures
Agree: meta-analyses show it causes higher performance across contexts
Disagree: studies find it adds nothing beyond transformational leadership
Qualify: links to engagement are consistent but mostly correlational
quiz.x: Studies using validated scales link servant leadership to engagement, trust and performance, and it explains outcomes beyond transformational leadership, but most work is correlational and effects vary by culture.

quiz.q: At all-staff meetings, a US bank's regional director praises his team humbly, but in executive reviews he presents their ideas as his own. Which element of genuine servant leadership does this most directly undermine?
opts: Trust, because his motive is image, which is the performer distortion
Conceptualisation, because he is losing sight of the long-range vision
Persuasion, because he is relying on positional power with executives
Empathy, because he has not tried to understand his team's motives
quiz.x: Humble language in public with self-serving control in private is the performer; credit is where motive shows under pressure. Persuasion is a plausible runner-up but nothing here concerns building agreement.

quiz.q: A 12-person health NGO in northern Cameroon has lost a donor and cannot hire. The director asks why servant leadership might matter more, not less, in this situation. What is the strongest reason?
opts: It lets the director delegate hard decisions to the team to share risk
It reduces the need for formal performance standards in small teams
Growing current staff's capability multiplies what a fixed team can do
It lowers wage expectations because staff are motivated by the mission
quiz.x: With no new hires, the leverage is developing current people and building commitment. Delegating hard decisions sounds empowering but shifts the leader's responsibility; servant leaders keep making hard calls.

quiz.q: A Lagos edtech company must cut 15 of 60 roles after a funding round collapses. Which approach is most consistent with servant leadership?
opts: Delay the decision until next quarter to protect morale while seeking new investors
Tell staff early and honestly, support leavers, and share the cuts visibly
Let each manager choose and announce cuts so decisions sit close to the teams
Announce the cuts by email to limit emotional disruption and avoid rumours
quiz.x: Servant leaders make hard decisions while considering people's needs: honesty, dignity, and leaders sharing the burden. Delaying is the runner-up but lets rumour and fear grow and may worsen the eventual cuts.

quiz.q: A Houston insurance firm's COO says that as AI handles more analysis, leadership will become purely technical. Using the course's argument, what is the best counterpoint?
opts: As tasks are automated, trust and people's growth become core to leading
Leaders should slow AI adoption to protect jobs until staff feel comfortable
Technical skills matter less, so leaders should focus mainly on motivation
AI tools need leaders who can personally write the prompts for every team
quiz.x: The course argues that as routine tasks shift to AI, the human work of developing people and building trust matters more. Slowing adoption is a misreading: honest transitions and reskilling, not delay, are taught.

quiz.q: Comfort, a programme manager in Accra, is choosing raters for her 360 degree assessment. Which choice will produce the most useful insight?
opts: Her direct reports alone, since they feel her leadership most directly
Her manager and peers, to keep the rating free of team politics
Her five closest colleagues, who know her work well and will be candid
A mix of manager, peers and reports, including some she finds difficult
quiz.x: A 360 recovers the external view across levels; comparing rater groups reveals patterns such as behaviour changing with hierarchy. Direct reports alone is the runner-up but removes the comparison that makes gaps visible.

facts.t: Robert Greenleaf coined 'servant leadership' in The Servant as Leader.
facts.more: His test: do those served grow as persons — healthier, wiser, freer, more autonomous, more likely to serve? Hitting targets while diminishing people fails it.

facts.t: Characteristics of servant leaders described by Larry Spears.
facts.more: Listening, empathy, healing, awareness, persuasion, conceptualisation, foresight, stewardship, commitment to growth, building community — most useful as observable behaviours.

facts.t: Meta-analysis: servant leadership explains outcomes beyond transformational leadership.
facts.more: Hoch and colleagues (2018) found servant leadership added explained variance where ethical and authentic leadership largely did not. Most studies remain correlational, and effects vary by context.

facts.t: 'Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant.'
facts.more: Spoken to disciples arguing over rank, followed in John 13 by the washing of feet. Greatness is redefined, not abolished.

modules.d: Reading feedback like a practitioner — blind spots, patterns, and the two behaviours that matter most.
modules.body:
Why self-awareness is the foundation

Research on self-awareness, including Tasha Eurich's work, distinguishes internal self-awareness (knowing your own values, emotions and patterns) from external self-awareness (knowing how others experience you). Most people overestimate both. Leaders are especially vulnerable: the more senior you become, the fewer people tell you the truth. A 360° assessment is a structured way to recover the external view that power quietly removes.

The Johari window

The Johari window maps what is known to you and to others. The open area is known to both. The blind spot is known to others but not to you. The hidden area is known to you but not to others. The unknown is known to neither. Growth comes from shrinking the blind spot through feedback and shrinking the hidden area through appropriate disclosure. Your 360° results are primarily a tool for the blind spot.

Reading your results like a practitioner

Raw scores are less useful than patterns. Work through your report in this order:

  1. Gaps between self and others. Where you rate yourself much higher than others do is a likely blind spot. Where you rate yourself much lower is a hidden strength — often something you undervalue.
  2. Differences between rater groups. If direct reports rate you lower than peers on listening, your behaviour may change with hierarchy. That pattern is more informative than the average.
  3. Signal versus noise. A single extreme comment is data, not a verdict. A theme repeated by several raters in different words is a signal.
  4. Written comments. They explain the numbers. Look for verbs — what people say you do — rather than adjectives.
The emotional reaction is normal. Most leaders move through surprise, defensiveness or rationalisation before acceptance. Do not respond to raters while defensive. Do not try to identify anonymous raters — that destroys future honesty. Wait at least 48 hours before deciding what the feedback means.

From many findings to two behaviours

The most common mistake after a 360° is trying to fix everything. Behavioural change consumes attention; leaders who choose eight goals change nothing. Choose two behaviours with the highest leverage: usually one blind spot that affects many people and one strength you can use more deliberately. Express each as an observable behaviour ("I will ask two questions before giving my view in team meetings"), not a trait ("be a better listener").

Closing the loop: feedforward

Marshall Goldsmith's feedforward method makes change visible. Thank your raters, tell a few key people the two behaviours you are working on, and ask them for one suggestion for the future — not a critique of the past. Every few weeks, ask the same people whether they have noticed a change. This does two things: it gives you ongoing data, and it changes people's perception, because others tend to notice what they have been asked to watch for.

Your personal SWOT

A personal SWOT applies strategic thinking to yourself. Strengths and weaknesses are internal and should draw on your 360° evidence, not just self-opinion. Opportunities and threats are external: changes in your field, your organisation, technology or your community. List three of each, then interpret the matrix with four questions: How can my strengths capture these opportunities? How can my strengths defend against these threats? Which weakness most limits an opportunity? Which weakness combined with a threat is my greatest risk? The interpretation, not the list, is the value.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Continue my Team21 Leadership Growth Journey. Act as my 360° debrief coach. I will paste my self-scores, rater-group scores and written comments. Identify the largest self-other gaps, differences between rater groups, and themes in the comments. Separate signal from noise. Then help me choose exactly two high-leverage behaviours, phrase them as observable actions, and build my personal SWOT with interpretation.

📚 Glossary

  • Internal / external self-awareness: knowing yourself / knowing how others experience you
  • Johari window: model of open, blind, hidden and unknown self-knowledge
  • Blind spot: something others see in you that you do not
  • Feedforward: asking for future-focused suggestions rather than critique of the past

📖 References

  • Eurich, T. (2017). Insight.
  • Luft, J. & Ingham, H. (1955). The Johari window.
  • Goldsmith, M. (2007). What Got You Here Won't Get You There.
  • Center for Creative Leadership — 360-degree feedback best practices.

quiz.q: Ahmed, a plant manager in Garoua, rates himself 4.6/5 on 'listens before deciding'. His direct reports give 2.9 and his peers give 4.2. What is the most useful interpretation?
opts: Direct reports usually rate managers lower, so the gap is expected
His listening may shift with hierarchy, a likely blind spot with reports
The average of 3.6 shows listening is a moderate, general weakness
The peer score confirms his view, so the low report score is likely noise
quiz.x: The lesson says differences between rater groups are more informative than the average; lower scores from reports than peers suggest behaviour changing with hierarchy. Averaging hides exactly that pattern.

quiz.q: In Sandra's 360 report, one anonymous comment calls her arrogant; no scores or other comments point that way. What is the best response?
opts: Set it aside as an outlier since one rater cannot represent the group
Make humility one of her two development goals since the word is so strong
Treat it as data and watch whether it appears as a repeated theme
Discuss the comment with the team to find out who wrote it and why
quiz.x: A single extreme comment is data, not a verdict; a theme repeated by several raters is signal. Dismissing it entirely is the runner-up but loses information; seeking the rater destroys future honesty.

quiz.q: After his 360, Kwame, a Kumasi school principal, writes eight development goals covering every low score. What is the most likely outcome?
opts: Improved trust, since raters see he took every comment seriously
Steady progress if he works on one goal per month over the next eight months
Fast progress, since covering every gap prevents any weakness being missed
Little real change, since behaviour change needs focus on a few goals
quiz.x: Behaviour change consumes attention; leaders with eight goals change nothing. Sequencing monthly is the runner-up but still spreads effort and ignores choosing the two highest-leverage behaviours.

quiz.q: A US hospital unit manager is drafting a development goal from her 360 results. Which version is phrased most effectively?
opts: Become a more patient and approachable leader for my nursing staff
Ask two questions before giving my view in each weekly team huddle
Read two books on listening and complete a coaching course this year
Improve my listening scores from 3.1 to 4.0 in next year's 360
quiz.x: Goals should be observable behaviours, not traits. The score target is the runner-up: measurable, but it names an outcome rather than the behaviour others will see.

quiz.q: Fatima rates herself 2.8 on 'developing others', but every rater group scores her above 4.3. Where does this sit in the Johari window and what does it suggest?
opts: A hidden strength she undervalues and could use more deliberately
The hidden area, so she should disclose more about her development work
A blind spot, so she should collect more feedback before accepting it
The open area, since raters and she both see development as relevant
quiz.x: Rating yourself much lower than others is a hidden strength; the lesson suggests choosing one strength to use more deliberately. 'Hidden area' is the runner-up but refers to things you know and others do not.

quiz.q: Two days after difficult 360 feedback, an operations director in Douala wants to email his team explaining why the low scores are unfair. What should he do?
opts: Send a shorter version that explains the context without naming scores
Ask HR to send it so the message reads as neutral rather than defensive
Wait 48 hours or more, then thank raters rather than rebut scores
Send it now, since quick transparency helps the team understand his view
quiz.x: The lesson warns not to respond while defensive and to wait at least 48 hours; the right next step is thanking raters and feedforward. A softened explanation is still a rebuttal that discourages future honesty.

quiz.q: Six weeks after her 360, a Chicago sales manager tells five colleagues she is working on two behaviours and asks each for one suggestion going forward. What is the main purpose of this feedforward?
opts: Letting raters explain their past criticisms in more detail and context
Showing her manager that she has completed the 360 process formally
Gathering future ideas, ongoing data, and making change visible
Replacing the next formal 360 with a cheaper informal version
quiz.x: Feedforward asks for future suggestions, provides ongoing data and shifts perception because people notice what they are asked to watch. Revisiting past critiques is the opposite of feedforward.

quiz.q: In his personal SWOT, Emmanuel lists 'my organisation is adopting AI tools rapidly' under Strengths. What is the main problem?
opts: It is an external change and belongs under Opportunities or Threats
It is fine there if he already uses AI tools well in his current role
It should be dropped because a SWOT should focus on personal traits
It belongs under Weaknesses because AI threatens many existing roles
quiz.x: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; changes in the organisation or technology are external. His own AI skill could be a strength, which makes the third option a tempting runner-up, but the item as written is external.

quiz.q: Nadia has finished listing three strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats and wants to find the single item combination that most endangers her career. Which interpretation question should she use?
opts: Which weakness most limits an opportunity I could otherwise capture?
Which of my weaknesses, paired with a threat, is the biggest danger?
How can my strengths defend against the threats I have listed?
Which threat is most likely to occur in the next twelve months?
quiz.x: The lesson names weakness plus threat as the greatest risk. Weakness limiting an opportunity is the runner-up: it shows a missed gain, not exposure to harm.

quiz.q: Jean was promoted from team lead to country director in Kinshasa and notices people now agree with him much more. What does self-awareness research suggest is happening?
opts: Staff are adapting to a new leader, and candour will return within months
His ideas have improved with experience, which is why agreement has risen
His internal self-awareness has grown, while external stays the same
He is receiving less honest feedback, so his self-view may be inflated
quiz.x: The more senior you become, the fewer people tell you the truth, and most people overestimate their self-awareness. The adaptation option is a plausible runner-up but ignores the structural effect of power.

facts.t: Share of people who met Tasha Eurich's criteria for being self-aware, despite most believing they are.
facts.more: Her team's research distinguishes internal from external self-awareness. Seniority makes the external view harder to get — fewer people tell you the truth.

facts.t: Quadrants of the Johari window: open, blind, hidden, unknown.
facts.more: Feedback shrinks the blind spot; appropriate disclosure shrinks the hidden area. A 360° is mainly a blind-spot tool.

facts.t: Minimum wait before deciding what your 360° feedback means.
facts.more: Surprise, defensiveness and rationalisation are normal first reactions. Never try to identify anonymous raters — it destroys future honesty.

facts.t: Behaviours to work on after a 360° — not eight.
facts.more: Pick one high-impact blind spot and one strength to use more deliberately, phrased as observable actions.

modules.d: Name what caps your growth, audit the seven areas of life, and write your leadership mission.
modules.body:
The lid principle

John Maxwell's "Law of the Lid" states that leadership ability determines a person's level of effectiveness — and, by extension, the effectiveness of the team and organisation they lead. A gifted team led by someone with a low lid on, say, decision-making or emotional control will underperform its talent. The practical question is not "Am I a good leader?" but "What specifically caps my effectiveness right now?"

Naming your lids honestly

Lids are usually not lack of knowledge. They tend to fall into five families:

  • Character lids — inconsistency between words and actions, cutting corners, unreliability.
  • Emotional lids — anger, anxiety, defensiveness, need for approval, fear of conflict.
  • Competence lids — a skill gap that now matters at your level (finance, strategy, public speaking, technology).
  • Relational lids — difficulty trusting, delegating, or building relationships beyond your circle.
  • Capacity lids — health, exhaustion, disorganisation, or a life so imbalanced that nothing has margin.

Use evidence — your 360°, recurring problems, feedback you have heard more than once — rather than introspection alone. A useful test: what keeps happening around me that I keep explaining as other people's fault? Repeated patterns usually point to a lid.

For each of your top three lids, define one action that would raise it within 90 days, one person who can hold you accountable, and one sign that would show it is rising. A lid named without an action is just a confession.

The seven-area life balance check

Leadership does not happen in a compartment. Neglect in one area of life eventually leaks into your leadership — through fatigue, distraction, irritability or poor judgement. Team21's life balance check asks whether you currently have intentional goals in seven areas:

  1. Spiritual life — your faith, values and sources of meaning.
  2. Family — your closest relationships and responsibilities.
  3. Finances — stability, stewardship, generosity and freedom from avoidable stress.
  4. Physical and mental health — sleep, movement, nutrition, rest and emotional wellbeing.
  5. Social life — friendships and community beyond work.
  6. Educational and professional growth — skills, credentials and career direction.
  7. Personal development — character, habits and the person you are becoming.

Score each from 1 to 10 for current satisfaction, and mark whether you have a written goal. Look for two things: the lowest score and any area where you scored high but have no goal — a strength you may be coasting on. Balance does not mean equal time in every area each week; seasons legitimately differ. It means no area is silently collapsing.

The leadership mission statement

No mission — no direction — no destination. A personal leadership mission statement answers: whom do I serve, what do I want to help them become or achieve, how will I lead, and what values are non-negotiable? Good statements are short enough to remember and specific enough to guide decisions. Compare "I want to be a great leader who helps people" with "I lead young professionals in my organisation to become confident, ethical decision-makers by coaching them honestly, sharing opportunities generously and refusing to win at the expense of integrity." The second can be used to make choices; the first cannot.

Testing your mission

Test the draft against three recent decisions. Would the mission have guided them? Does it explain how you will spend your time next month? Would the people closest to you recognise it as true of you, or only of who you want to become? Refine until the answer is yes — or until the gap is honestly named as growth work.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Continue my Team21 Leadership Growth Journey. Act as my leadership-lid diagnostician. Ask me about recurring problems, feedback I have heard more than once, and situations where I lose effectiveness. Identify my likely top three lids by family (character, emotional, competence, relational, capacity). Then run my 7-area life balance check one area at a time, and help me draft and stress-test a personal leadership mission statement.

📚 Glossary

  • Law of the Lid: leadership ability sets the ceiling on effectiveness
  • Capacity lid: a limit caused by health, exhaustion, disorganisation or imbalance
  • Life balance check: Team21's audit of seven life areas for satisfaction and intentional goals
  • Leadership mission statement: a short, decision-guiding statement of whom you serve, how and why

📖 References

  • Maxwell, J. C. (1998). The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership.
  • Covey, S. R. (1989). The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People — personal mission statements.
  • Team21 Academy, Leadership Growth Journey.

quiz.q: A department head at a Douala port operator finds three of her teams have each failed to escalate problems early. She attributes it to weak staff. What is the most useful reflection?
opts: Send all three teams on an escalation procedures course this quarter
Ask whether a repeated pattern around her points to her own lid
Add a weekly escalation report so problems surface on schedule
Replace the team leads, since the pattern shows a hiring weakness
quiz.x: The lesson's test: what keeps happening around me that I explain as others' fault? Repeated patterns usually point to a lid, such as how she reacts to bad news. The report is the runner-up but treats symptoms.

quiz.q: During his course, a Yaounde bank manager writes 'my lid is impatience' but defines no action, accountability partner or indicator. How does the course describe this?
opts: A confession: naming a lid without action changes nothing
A good first step, since naming a lid is most of the work
A capacity lid, since impatience usually reflects fatigue
An emotional lid that should be handed to a counsellor
quiz.x: The course says a lid named without an action is just a confession; each top lid needs a 90-day action, an accountability person and a sign of progress. Calling it 'most of the work' overstates naming.

quiz.q: An Atlanta product manager works 75-hour weeks, sleeps five hours a night, and has become irritable in meetings. Which lid family is most evident?
opts: Character, because irritability shows a gap between words and acts
Competence, because he cannot finish work in normal hours
Emotional, because irritability in meetings is the visible issue
Capacity, because exhaustion and imbalance leave no margin
quiz.x: Capacity lids include exhaustion and imbalanced life. Emotional is the runner-up, but here the irritability is a symptom of the capacity problem, which is where action belongs.

quiz.q: Bih scores 9/10 on educational and professional growth in the seven-area check, but has no written goal in that area. What does the course suggest this may indicate?
opts: A sign the score is inflated and should be lowered
An area where she is overinvesting at the cost of family
A strength she may be coasting on, worth setting a goal for
A balanced area that needs no further attention for now
quiz.x: The course flags high scores without goals as possible coasting. Leaving it alone is the runner-up, but balance means intentional goals, not just current satisfaction.

quiz.q: With his spouse's agreement, a Lagos engineer spends far more time at work than at home for six weeks of a product launch, then returns to normal. Is this a balance failure by the course's standard?
opts: Not necessarily: seasons differ if nothing collapses
Yes, since every area needs equal attention each week
Yes, because family should outrank work at all times
No, as long as his professional goals are met on time
quiz.x: Balance does not mean equal time each week; seasons legitimately differ, provided no area is silently collapsing. The last option is a runner-up but judges by work results, not by the health of other areas.

quiz.q: Four participants share draft leadership mission statements. Which is most useful for guiding decisions?
opts: I aim to become a director within five years and lead a large hospital
I coach new nurses to become confident, safe practitioners by teaching honestly
I lead with integrity, excellence, humility and passion every single day
I want to be a great leader who helps people reach their full potential
quiz.x: A useful mission names whom you serve, what they become, how you lead and values. The value list is the runner-up: it has values but no one served and no outcome, so it cannot guide choices.

quiz.q: Ruth, an operations lead in Kigali, has drafted her leadership mission statement. How should she test it?
opts: Keep it for a year and see whether it still feels right afterwards
Compare it with the mission statement of her organisation for alignment
Check whether it would have guided three recent decisions
Ask three colleagues to rate how inspiring the wording sounds
quiz.x: The lesson tests a draft against three recent decisions, next month's time, and whether close people would recognise it. Alignment with the organisation is reasonable but is not the course's test.

quiz.q: A participant asks why a leadership course includes family, finances and health. Which answer best reflects the course?
opts: Organisations are responsible for managing all areas of employees' lives
These areas are personal, but faith-based programmes usually include them
Balanced leaders are more likeable, which makes persuasion easier
Neglect in one area leaks into leadership through fatigue or poor judgement
quiz.x: The course argues leadership is not compartmentalised; neglect leaks into judgement and energy. The likeability option is plausible but is not the mechanism the lesson describes.

quiz.q: Samuel, a project manager in Buea, is under heavy personal debt stress and has been avoiding conversations about budget overruns on his project. How does the life-balance view help?
opts: It suggests keeping personal matters separate from project discussions
It shows he has a competence lid in finance that needs formal training first
It suggests he should hand the budget to a colleague until his debts clear
It shows his finances are affecting his work and need an intentional goal
quiz.x: The life-balance check names finances as an area that leaks into leadership. A competence lid is the runner-up, but the avoidance stems from stress in his own finances, not a skill gap.

quiz.q: A newly promoted manager in Abidjan has read widely on delegation yet still keeps doing tasks herself because she fears her team will make mistakes. Why does the course treat this as a lid rather than a knowledge gap?
opts: Because lids are usually patterns like fear or distrust, not missing facts
Because her organisation lacks a clear delegation policy for managers
Because delegation is a competence lid that improves with more reading
Because she has not yet attended a structured delegation training course
quiz.x: Lids are usually not lack of knowledge; this is a relational or emotional lid (difficulty trusting). The competence option is the runner-up, but she already has the knowledge.

facts.t: The Law of the Lid opens Maxwell's 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership.
facts.more: Leadership ability sets the ceiling on effectiveness — for the leader and the team. The useful question is: what specifically caps me right now?

facts.t: Lid families: character, emotional, competence, relational, capacity.
facts.more: Lids are rarely about lack of knowledge. Repeated patterns you keep blaming on others usually point to one.

facts.t: Areas in Team21's life balance check.
facts.more: Spiritual, family, finances, physical and mental health, social, educational/professional, personal development. Look for the lowest score and any high score with no written goal.

facts.t: Horizon for one action to raise each of your top three lids.
facts.more: Each lid also needs an accountability person and a visible sign of progress. A lid named without an action is just a confession.

labs.title: Name the lid family
labs.intro: Each statement comes from a leader's honest reflection. Which lid family is it?
items: I promise reports by Friday and often deliver Tuesday
I snap at staff when donors criticise us
I avoid hard conversations because I need to be liked
I can't read a cash-flow statement now that I run the whole NGO
Our digital tools have outgrown my skills
I only delegate to the two people I've known for ten years
I work until 1 a.m., sleep five hours and miss my children's events
My desk and inbox are so disorganised that deadlines slip
labs.tip: The same symptom (missed deadlines) can come from different lids — look for the root pattern.

labs.title: Spot the weak points in this mission and lid plan
labs.intro: A youth pastor in Buea drafted this. Tap the parts that would not guide decisions or produce change.
segments: Mission: I want to be a great leader who helps people.
Too vague to guide choices — whom, to become what, how, with which values?
I serve the 40 young adults in our church's career ministry,
helping them become confident, ethical professionals by coaching honestly and sharing opportunities.
Top lid: I get defensive when criticised.
Action: try to be better about it.
Not an action — needs one specific behaviour within 90 days.
Accountability: Elder Nfor will ask me monthly about it.
Life balance: all seven areas scored 8, so no goals are needed.
High scores with no written goal may hide coasting; balance needs intentional goals.
Second lid: I keep explaining missed deadlines as my volunteers' fault.
Sign of progress: I will feel better.
A feeling is not observable — pick a sign others could see.
labs.tip: Good missions and lid plans are specific enough to make a decision with.

modules.d: The three mechanics of everyday leadership — practised before the real conversations.
modules.body:
Trust is built from three things people observe

Mayer, Davis and Schoorman's widely cited model holds that trust rests on perceptions of ability (can you do what you say?), benevolence (do you care about my interests?) and integrity (do you keep principles I accept?). Leaders often over-invest in ability and neglect the other two. People may respect a brilliant manager whom they do not trust to protect them, keep confidences or tell the truth.

Trust is built in small, repeated behaviours: keeping minor promises, admitting mistakes quickly, giving credit publicly and taking blame publicly, being consistent between what you say to someone's face and behind their back, and extending trust first in proportion to the risk. It is lost much faster than it is built — usually through a single betrayal of integrity.

Psychological safety

Amy Edmondson defines psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — asking questions, admitting errors, raising concerns. Her research, and Google's Project Aristotle, found it among the strongest predictors of team effectiveness. Psychological safety is not comfort or low standards; the most effective teams combine high safety with high accountability. Leaders build it by framing work as learning, acknowledging their own fallibility, inviting input explicitly, and — critically — responding well when someone brings bad news. One defensive reaction teaches the whole team to stay silent.

Feedback that people can use

The Situation–Behaviour–Impact (SBI) model from the Center for Creative Leadership keeps feedback specific and non-judgemental: describe the situation (when and where), the observable behaviour (what the person did or said — not your interpretation of their character), and the impact (what effect it had). Then — the step most people skip — ask and listen: "What was going on from your side?" Finally, agree on the next step together.

Compare. "You're careless with client reports." versus "In Tuesday's report to the clinic board (S), three figures in the budget table didn't match the finance system (B). The chair questioned our credibility in front of the funder (I). What happened on your end?" The first invites defensiveness; the second invites problem-solving.

Praise deserves the same specificity. "Great job" is pleasant but uninformative; "The way you summarised the three options on one page let the board decide in ten minutes" teaches what to repeat. Aim for frequent, timely, private correction and specific, sincere recognition — publicly where the person welcomes it.

Delegation that develops people

Delegation is not dumping unwanted tasks. Developmental delegation transfers responsibility and authority in a way that grows the person. Match the level of delegation to the person's competence and commitment on this task — the core insight of situational leadership: a highly capable but newly assigned person may need direction on an unfamiliar task, while a long-serving expert needs autonomy. Typical levels range from "do exactly this", through "recommend, then I decide", "decide and tell me", to "decide and act; tell me only if there's a problem".

Good delegation states the outcome and why it matters, the constraints (budget, deadline, non-negotiables), the authority granted, the check-in points, and the support available. The classic failure is reverse delegation: the person brings the problem back and the leader takes it ("leave it with me"). A servant leader asks, "What do you recommend?" and coaches toward their solution.

Difficult conversations

Every leader eventually must address underperformance, misconduct or conflict. Prepare by separating facts from interpretations, clarifying the outcome you want for the person and the organisation, and anticipating emotions — theirs and yours. Open with purpose, describe the facts, listen genuinely, problem-solve together, and close with clear agreements. Practise first: rehearsing aloud, or with an AI simulation, reduces the chance that emotion hijacks the real conversation.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a difficult-conversation simulator. I will describe a team member and a performance or conduct issue. Play that person realistically — including defensiveness, emotion or excuses based on the context. Let me practise opening with SBI, listening and agreeing next steps. After the conversation, give me feedback on clarity, empathy, accountability and whether I took the problem back (reverse delegation).

📚 Glossary

  • Ability / benevolence / integrity: the three perceived bases of trust
  • Psychological safety: shared belief that interpersonal risk-taking is safe
  • SBI: Situation–Behaviour–Impact feedback model
  • Reverse delegation: the leader taking back a task the team member should own
  • Situational leadership: matching leadership style to the person's competence and commitment on a task

📖 References

  • Mayer, R., Davis, J. & Schoorman, F. (1995). An integrative model of organizational trust. Academy of Management Review.
  • Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly; The Fearless Organization (2018).
  • Center for Creative Leadership — SBI feedback model.
  • Hersey, P. & Blanchard, K. — Situational Leadership.
  • Stone, D., Patton, B. & Heen, S. Difficult Conversations.

quiz.q: A Douala telecom engineering manager is technically brilliant and respected, yet his team hides mistakes because he brings them up months later. Which trust element is weakest?
opts: Ability, because they doubt he can solve problems
Benevolence, as they doubt he protects their interests
Competence, because he lacks people-management skill
Integrity, because he breaks principles he states
quiz.x: In the Mayer, Davis and Schoorman model, benevolence is whether he cares about their interests. His ability is clear; integrity is a runner-up, but nothing shows him breaking stated principles.

quiz.q: At 9 pm before a board submission, an analyst at a Johannesburg fund flags a data error. The director snaps at her in front of the team. What is the most significant consequence?
opts: The analyst may hesitate, but others will understand the deadline pressure
The analyst should have raised it earlier, which the director has signalled
The team learns that raising bad news is risky and will stay silent
The board pack will be late, which will damage the fund's credibility
quiz.x: Edmondson's point: one defensive reaction teaches the whole team to stay silent. The deadline-pressure option is the runner-up, but safety depends on how bad news is received regardless of pressure.

quiz.q: A clinic manager in Bafoussam must give feedback on a report with errors. Which statement best follows SBI?
opts: Your reports need more attention because the board is losing confidence
You're careless with reports, and the board has noticed it again this month
In Monday's report you seemed rushed and unfocused, which the chair noticed
In Monday's report, three figures didn't match finance, and the chair queried us
quiz.x: SBI: situation, observable behaviour, impact. The 'rushed and unfocused' option is the runner-up: it has a situation and impact but gives an interpretation instead of observable behaviour.

quiz.q: A Phoenix team leader has just described situation, behaviour and impact to an employee about missed deadlines. What should she do next?
opts: Ask what was going on from his side, listen, then agree next steps
State the consequences if the deadlines are missed again this quarter
Offer specific suggestions so he leaves with a clear improvement plan
Close the meeting and send a written summary of the feedback given
quiz.x: The step most people skip is asking and listening, then agreeing next steps together. Offering suggestions is the runner-up but jumps to solutions before understanding his side.

quiz.q: Ngozi, a senior engineer with fifteen years' experience, is assigned to lead a vendor negotiation for the first time. Which delegation level fits best at the start?
opts: Decide and act, telling her manager just if a problem arises
Decide on terms and inform her manager after signing
Recommend a negotiating position, then her manager decides
Do exactly as the manager scripts, word for word
quiz.x: Situational leadership matches delegation to competence on this task, not general seniority. Full autonomy suits her engineering work, not a first negotiation; scripting is too controlling for someone this capable.

quiz.q: A grants officer in Bamenda tells her director she is stuck on the funder report and asks him to look. He replies, 'Leave it with me.' What has happened?
opts: Situational leadership, since he is adjusting to her low competence
Reverse delegation: the problem has moved back to the leader
Supportive delegation, since he is removing a blocker for her
Good stewardship, since the funder relationship is at risk
quiz.x: Taking the problem back is reverse delegation; a servant leader coaches the person to solve it. 'Removing a blocker' sounds helpful but costs her growth and his time.

quiz.q: A New York agency head says her team has high psychological safety because nobody is ever criticised and deadlines are relaxed. Which response is most accurate?
opts: She is right: safety means a comfortable, low-pressure team climate
She is confusing safety with trust, which is a separate issue in the trust model
She is confusing safety with comfort; strong teams pair it with accountability
She is right, though safety matters less than technical skill in most teams
quiz.x: Edmondson: psychological safety is safety for interpersonal risk, not comfort or low standards; top teams combine it with accountability. The trust option is a runner-up but misses the comfort error.

quiz.q: A Yaounde NGO director delegates a donor event to a coordinator, explaining the goal and deadline. Two weeks later they clash over spending decisions. Which element was most likely missing?
opts: A detailed task list for each stage of the event planning
Clarity on authority granted and limits such as budget
The reason the event matters to the organisation's mission
Praise for the coordinator's previous successful events
quiz.x: Good delegation states outcome, constraints, authority, check-ins and support. The clash over spending shows authority and budget limits were unclear. The task list is a runner-up but would micromanage.

quiz.q: A Lagos sales director must address a colleague who has been late to three client meetings this month. Which preparation step is most valuable?
opts: Draft a warning letter in case the conversation goes badly
Review his personnel file for any earlier pattern of lateness
Ask other team members how they feel about his punctuality
Collect the specific dates, what happened and the client effect
quiz.x: SBI needs concrete situations, behaviour and impact. Asking colleagues is a runner-up but brings hearsay and interpretation instead of observable facts.

quiz.q: After a board meeting in Accra, a manager wants to praise an analyst. Which praise is most likely to reinforce the desired behaviour?
opts: Your one-page summary of three options let the board decide fast
You are one of the most talented analysts on our whole team
Thank you for all the extra hours you put into preparing for today
Great job today, the board was clearly impressed with your work
quiz.x: Specific praise teaches what to repeat. Thanking extra hours is a runner-up but reinforces effort rather than the behaviour that produced the result.

facts.t: Bases of trust: ability, benevolence, integrity.
facts.more: Mayer, Davis and Schoorman (1995). Leaders often over-invest in ability; people may respect a brilliant manager they do not trust to protect them.

facts.t: Psychological safety ranked first among team dynamics in Google's Project Aristotle.
facts.more: It builds on Amy Edmondson's 1999 research. It is not comfort: the best teams pair high safety with high accountability.

facts.t: Situation, Behaviour, Impact — then ask and listen.
facts.more: From the Center for Creative Leadership. Describe observable behaviour, not character; the step most people skip is asking 'What was going on from your side?'

facts.t: Delegation from 'do exactly this' to 'decide and act'.
facts.more: Match the level to the person's competence and commitment on this task — the core of situational leadership. Resist reverse delegation: ask 'What do you recommend?'

plaibox.title: Simulation: the difficult conversation
plaibox.intro: You lead a programme team in Yaoundé. Your M&E officer, Brenda, has missed two data deadlines and was curt with a partner. Score: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

Mention it in the weekly team meeting so all learn

Shuts down listening and misses a real cause.
Ask how often it happens and what she has tried

Agree the partner is the real problem

Warm, but without clear agreements change is unlikely.
Warn her that a third miss means a formal process

modules.t: Leading in the AI Era & Through Adversity
modules.d: Leading when resources are thin and stakes are high — and leading people honestly through technological change.
modules.body:
Adversity reveals and forms leaders

Leadership in comfortable conditions is mostly management. Adversity — funding cuts, crises, political instability, loss, failure — reveals character and, if handled well, forms it. Leaders who have built institutions across difficult environments tend to learn the same lessons: clarity about what truly matters, honesty about reality, relentless focus on the few things that keep the mission alive, and care for people who are carrying fear.

The Stockdale paradox

Jim Collins, in Good to Great, describes the Stockdale paradox, drawn from Admiral James Stockdale's survival as a prisoner of war: retain unwavering faith that you will prevail in the end, while confronting the most brutal facts of your current reality. Stockdale observed that the optimists who expected release "by Christmas" were crushed when it did not come. Hope without realism breaks people; realism without hope paralyses them. Leaders in adversity must hold both — and communicate both.

"Count it all joy… when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness." — James 1:2–3. For leaders of faith, adversity is not only a problem to solve but a place where character is forged.

Leading when resources are thin

Practical disciplines for constrained environments: Protect the core — identify the activities without which the mission dies and defend them. Simplify ruthlessly — stop good activities to fund essential ones. Communicate more, not less — silence during uncertainty is filled with rumour. Share the burden visibly — leaders who take the first cut earn the right to ask for sacrifice. Build partnerships — pooled capability with other organisations often beats solitary survival. Look after people — fear narrows thinking; acknowledging it openly restores capacity.

Resilience is a team property, not just a personal trait

Personal resilience draws on purpose, relationships, physical recovery and the ability to reframe setbacks as temporary and specific rather than permanent and pervasive. But leaders build organisational resilience too: cross-training so no single person is a point of failure, reserves of time and money, documented processes, diverse funding, and a culture that learns from failure instead of hiding it.

How AI is changing work and teams

Generative AI is changing tasks before it changes whole jobs. In most roles, some tasks are automated, many are augmented, and new tasks emerge — prompting, reviewing AI output, managing data quality, judging ethical risks. Leaders must therefore think task by task: which activities in each role are changing, what new skills are needed, and how time freed by automation will be redeployed to higher-value work.

Three leadership responsibilities follow. Honest transitions: tell people the truth about how roles are likely to change, as early as possible, rather than promising "nothing will change" or allowing fear to grow in silence. Real reskilling: invest time and money in training, coaching and practice — not a single webinar. Human-centred governance: set clear rules for responsible use — data privacy, accuracy checking, transparency with clients, accountability for decisions that remain human.

Motivation and meaning in AI-augmented teams

When routine work disappears, people may feel either liberated or threatened. Self-determination theory suggests motivation rests on autonomy, competence and relatedness. AI can strengthen all three — freeing time for meaningful work and building new skills — or weaken them, if people feel replaced, deskilled or isolated. The leader's design choices decide which happens. Involve teams in deciding how tools are used; recognise new skills; keep human connection central.

Leading with both truth and hope

Adversity and technological change call for the same leadership posture: honest about reality, committed to people, anchored in purpose, and active rather than passive. Servant leaders do not shield people from truth; they walk with them through it.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are my AI-transition strategist. I will describe my team's roles. For each role, break the work into tasks and classify each as likely automated, augmented or unchanged by AI in the next two years, with new tasks that may emerge. Then help me draft an honest team communication about the changes, a 90-day reskilling plan, and three responsible-use rules for our context.

📚 Glossary

  • Stockdale paradox: faith that you will prevail combined with confronting brutal facts
  • Task-level analysis: examining which activities in a role change, rather than the whole job
  • Augmentation: AI assisting a human who retains judgement and accountability
  • Self-determination theory: motivation from autonomy, competence and relatedness
  • Organisational resilience: an organisation's capacity to absorb shocks and adapt

📖 References

  • Collins, J. (2001). Good to Great.
  • Deci, E. & Ryan, R. — Self-determination theory.
  • Brynjolfsson, E. & McAfee, A. — work on technology, tasks and productivity.
  • Team21 Academy, AI Unlocked curriculum.

quiz.q: During a funding crisis, a Nairobi NGO director tells staff, 'Everything will be resolved by next quarter', with no evidence. When it is not, morale collapses. Which principle was violated?
opts: The Stockdale paradox: faith in the end must be held with the brutal facts
Sharing the burden: he should have taken the first salary cut himself
Protecting the core: he should have defended the essential programmes first
Building partnerships: he should have pooled resources with other NGOs
quiz.x: Optimists expecting release 'by Christmas' were crushed; hope must be paired with confronting reality. The other options are valid practices but do not explain why false optimism broke morale.

quiz.q: A Douala manufacturing company must cut costs by 20%. Which action most builds credibility for asking staff to sacrifice?
opts: Announcing a detailed plan showing every department cuts the same 20%
Senior leaders take the first, visible pay cut before asking others
Offering staff a bonus once the company returns to profitability
Hiring an outside consultant to decide the cuts to ensure neutrality
quiz.x: Leaders who take the first cut earn the right to ask for sacrifice. Equal cuts look fair but ignore protecting the core and do not show leaders sharing the burden first.

quiz.q: Staff at a Dallas hospital are anxious about rumoured restructuring, and leadership plans to say nothing until plans are final in three months. What is the most likely result?
opts: Little effect, since staff expect confidentiality during restructuring
Better final decisions, since leaders can consider options privately
Calm, since staff will not worry about plans that are not yet decided
Rumour fills the silence, fear grows and good people may leave early
quiz.x: Silence during uncertainty is filled with rumour; communicate more, not less. Private deliberation is a runner-up benefit but does not justify silence on what is known.

quiz.q: Aisha leads a 10-person accounts team in Kano and wants to plan for AI. Which approach is most useful?
opts: Estimate how many of the 10 roles AI will replace over the next three years
Wait for the finance director's AI policy before taking any steps herself
Ask which tasks in each role are automated, augmented or new
Buy the leading AI accounting tool and let staff learn it on the job
quiz.x: AI changes tasks before jobs, so leaders think task by task and plan skills and redeployment. Counting replaced roles is the runner-up but uses the wrong unit of analysis.

quiz.q: A Lagos bank CEO tells staff 'AI will not change anyone's job here', although plans exist to automate part of customer service. What is the most serious leadership failure?
opts: A failure of reskilling, since no training budget has been announced yet
A failure of foresight, since he has misjudged how fast AI is developing
A failure of governance, since AI risks have not been assessed in writing
A failure of honest transitions, damaging trust when plans emerge
quiz.x: He knows the truth and is withholding it; the course asks for honest, early transitions. Reskilling is a runner-up gap but the core failure is the false promise.

quiz.q: A US accounting firm launches AI tools with one one-hour webinar and expects productivity gains within a month. Which responsibility is most neglected?
opts: Real reskilling through training, coaching and practice
Honest transitions about how roles will change in future
Protecting the core activities the firm depends on most
Human-centred governance over privacy and accuracy checks
quiz.x: The course says real reskilling means time and money for training, coaching and practice, not a single webinar. Governance matters too but the scenario's gap is skill-building.

quiz.q: After AI drafting tools arrive, editors at a Johannesburg publisher say they feel 'replaced and pointless'. Under self-determination theory, which need is most likely unmet?
opts: Autonomy, because management chose the tools without them
Competence, because their skills no longer feel valued or used
Relatedness, because they now work more with AI than colleagues
Security, because they fear losing their jobs to the new tools
quiz.x: Feeling pointless and replaced signals lost competence. Autonomy is a plausible runner-up but the complaint is about value of their skills; security is not one of the three SDT needs.

quiz.q: A 15-person NGO in Maroua depends on one finance officer who alone knows how to file donor reports. Which practice most improves its resilience?
opts: Raise the finance officer's salary to reduce the risk of departure
Hire an external auditor to review donor reports each year
Cross-train a second person and document the reporting steps
Build a three-month cash reserve against delays in funding
quiz.x: Cross-training removes a single point of failure, which is the risk described. Reserves also build resilience but do not address dependence on one person.

quiz.q: A Washington consultant uses AI to draft client recommendations and sends them without review; a factual error damages the relationship. Which governance rule was missing?
opts: Accuracy checks with a human accountable for the output
Data privacy rules for uploading client files to AI tools
A policy restricting AI use to internal documents for now
Transparency telling the client that AI was used in drafting
quiz.x: Human-centred governance includes accuracy checking and human accountability. Transparency is a runner-up, but disclosure would not have prevented the error.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian university vice-rector faces both budget cuts and rapid AI adoption. Which posture best serves her people through both?
opts: Decisive, cutting fast and adopting AI fast to get through the change quickly
Honest about hard facts, hopeful about the future, investing in people
Optimistic and reassuring to keep fear low until the situation becomes clearer
Cautious, pausing AI adoption until the budget position stabilises
quiz.x: Stockdale realism with hope, plus honest transitions and reskilling, serve people in both challenges. Pausing AI is a cautious runner-up but delays the honest preparation people need.

facts.t: Time Admiral James Stockdale spent as a prisoner of war in Vietnam (1965–73).
facts.more: Jim Collins drew the Stockdale paradox from him: unwavering faith you will prevail, plus confronting the brutal facts. The optimists who expected release 'by Christmas' broke.

facts.t: Self-determination theory: autonomy, competence, relatedness.
facts.more: AI can strengthen all three by freeing time for meaningful work — or weaken them if people feel replaced, deskilled or isolated. Design choices decide which.

facts.t: Generative AI changes tasks before it changes whole jobs.
facts.more: In most roles some tasks are automated, many augmented, and new ones emerge — prompting, reviewing output, data quality, ethical judgement. Analyse task by task.

facts.t: 'The testing of your faith produces steadfastness.'
facts.more: For leaders of faith, adversity is not only a problem to solve but a place where character is forged.

modules.d: Pray · Plan · People — a six-month plan, mentor-reviewed and accountability-scheduled.
modules.body:
From insight to sustained change

Most leadership development fails at the same point: participants leave with insight but no structure to turn it into habit. Research on behaviour change consistently finds that intentions alone rarely produce lasting change; specific plans, environmental cues, social support and regular review do. Your capstone integrates everything from the past five weeks — your identity answers, 360° findings, SWOT, lids, life balance and mission — into a six-month Personal Growth Plan built on the Team21 3Ps: Pray, Plan, People.

P1 — Pray: your anchoring practices

Leaders under pressure drift unless anchored. "Pray" names the practices that keep you connected to your deepest values and source of strength. For Christian leaders, this includes prayer, Scripture, worship and reflection on how faith shapes leadership. For every participant, it includes regular practices of reflection — journaling, silence, a weekly review — that keep the mission statement alive rather than filed away. Define when, where and how long; anchoring practices tied to a specific time and place survive busy weeks far better than good intentions.

"Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labour in vain." — Psalm 127:1. A plan without an anchor tends to serve ambition rather than calling.

P2 — Plan: SMART goals with quarterly milestones

Translate your two high-leverage behaviours, your top lid actions and your lowest life-balance area into goals that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Then break each into quarterly milestones and weekly actions. Use implementation intentions — "When situation X occurs, I will do Y" — which research by Peter Gollwitzer shows substantially increases follow-through. Example: "When I enter a team meeting where a decision is needed, I will ask two questions before stating my view."

Limit the plan. Three to five goals across six months is ambitious enough. Include at least one leading indicator per goal — something you control and can track weekly (number of coaching conversations held) — alongside lagging indicators that show results over time (360° listening score, staff retention).

P3 — People: mentorship and accountability

No leader grows alone. Your plan names three kinds of people. A mentor who has walked further ahead and will review your plan and progress honestly. An accountability partner — often a peer — who checks in regularly on specific commitments. And observers — people affected by your behaviour whom you ask, through feedforward, whether they notice change. Schedule these conversations now, with dates in the calendar, before graduation. Commitments without dates rarely happen.

Building in review and adjustment

A good plan expects obstacles. Hold a brief weekly review (what did I do, what got in the way, what will I do next week?), a monthly check with your accountability partner, and a quarterly review with your mentor — adjusting goals when circumstances change, without abandoning the direction. Plan in advance what you will do after a missed week: "If I miss my weekly review, I will do it the next morning before email." Recovery plans prevent one lapse becoming the end of the plan.

Your capstone deliverable

  1. Your leadership mission statement (refined).
  2. Summary of insights: 360° themes, SWOT interpretation, top three lids, life-balance scores.
  3. Pray: anchoring practices with time, place and duration.
  4. Plan: three to five SMART goals, each with quarterly milestones, implementation intentions and leading and lagging indicators.
  5. People: named mentor, accountability partner and observers, with scheduled review dates.
  6. Your obstacle and recovery plan.

Your mentor reviews the plan one-to-one before graduation and confirms the review calendar. Graduation is not the end of the programme — it is the start of the six months that matter most.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Complete my Team21 Leadership Growth Journey. Act as my Personal Growth Plan architect. Using my mission statement, 360° themes, SWOT, top lids and life-balance scores (which I will paste), help me build a six-month plan on the 3Ps: Pray (anchoring practices with time and place), Plan (3–5 SMART goals with quarterly milestones, implementation intentions, leading and lagging indicators) and People (mentor, accountability partner, observers with dates). Then stress-test it against likely obstacles.

📚 Glossary

  • 3Ps: Team21's growth framework: Pray, Plan, People
  • Implementation intention: an if-then plan linking a situation to a specific action
  • Leading indicator: a controllable activity measured frequently
  • Lagging indicator: a result that shows change over time
  • Accountability partner: a peer who checks commitments regularly

📖 References

  • Gollwitzer, P. (1999). Implementation intentions. American Psychologist.
  • Clear, J. (2018). Atomic Habits.
  • Doran, G. (1981). There's a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management's goals. Management Review.
  • Team21 Academy, Leadership Growth Journey and the 3Ps.

quiz.q: Linda writes in her growth plan, 'I will reflect more on my leadership.' Which change would most increase the chance she follows through?
opts: Share the goal on social media to create public commitment
Add a reason explaining why reflection matters to her as a leader
Raise the goal to reflect daily so the habit forms more quickly
Specify when, where and how long, e.g. Sunday 7 pm for 20 minutes
quiz.x: Anchoring practices tied to specific time and place survive busy weeks. Adding a reason helps motivation but does not create the cue that triggers action.

quiz.q: Tunde, a Lagos operations lead, is drafting goals for his six-month growth plan. Which goal is closest to a well-formed SMART goal with an implementation intention?
opts: I will improve my 360 listening score from 3.1 to 4.0 by the next assessment
I will read two books on listening and practise their ideas over six months
When a meeting needs a decision, I ask two questions before my view, until June
I will become a much better listener in team meetings by the end of this year
quiz.x: An implementation intention uses 'when X, I will do Y'. The score target is SMART-like and the runner-up, but it lacks the situational cue and names an outcome.

quiz.q: A participant in Buea lists nine goals for the next six months. What is the most appropriate mentor feedback?
opts: Keep all nine because ambition shows commitment to growth
Cut to three to five goals so attention can produce real change
Spread them so three are tackled in each of the next three months
Keep all nine but rank them so the top three get the most time
quiz.x: The course says three to five goals across six months is ambitious enough. Ranking is the runner-up but still leaves too many active commitments competing for attention.

quiz.q: Aminata, a Yaounde finance manager, has a six-month goal of improving her listening. Which is a leading indicator she can track weekly?
opts: Meetings where she asked two questions before giving her view
Number of compliments on her listening she receives this quarter
Staff retention in her team at the end of the financial year
Her listening score on the next 360 assessment in six months' time
quiz.x: Leading indicators are things you control and track weekly. The 360 score and retention are lagging; compliments are not under her control.

quiz.q: A Houston programme asks participants to book mentor and accountability dates before graduation day. Why?
opts: Early dates let mentors prepare formal written assessments
Mentors are busy, so early booking secures the best time slots for them
Commitments without dates rarely happen once normal work resumes
Graduation certificates require proof of a scheduled mentor
quiz.x: The course states commitments without dates rarely happen. Mentor availability is a plausible runner-up but misses the behaviour-change point.

quiz.q: A participant in Kigali misses two weekly reviews during a busy month and decides the plan has failed. Which capstone element would have helped most?
opts: A monthly mentor review held in place of the weekly reviews
A larger number of goals so one lapse matters less to the whole plan
A firmer personal commitment to not missing any weekly review again
A pre-planned recovery rule, like doing a missed review next morning
quiz.x: Recovery plans prevent one lapse becoming the end of the plan. A stricter commitment sounds disciplined but sets up the same collapse after the next miss.

quiz.q: How does the course frame the main purpose of the 'Pray' element for leaders under pressure?
opts: A weekly to-do review that tracks progress on SMART goals
A way to reduce stress so leaders can work longer hours
A requirement that all participants adopt Christian practices
Anchoring practices that keep leaders tied to their values
quiz.x: Pray names anchoring practices, including reflection for every participant, that keep the mission alive. A weekly review is part of it but is not its purpose; it does not require any faith.

quiz.q: Peter's plan includes a mentor and three observers from his team. Why include observers in addition to the mentor?
opts: They see his behaviour directly and can say whether change is visible
They help him decide which goals to drop if the plan becomes too large
They can stand in for the mentor if the mentor is too busy to meet monthly
They provide a formal rating that counts toward course certification
quiz.x: Observers are people affected by his behaviour, asked through feedforward whether they notice change. The mentor reviews the plan but does not see daily behaviour.

quiz.q: Halfway through her plan, Esther is promoted to regional manager in Douala and one goal no longer fits. What should she do?
opts: Abandon the plan and write a new one suited to the new role
Pause all goals until she has settled into the new role
Adjust the goal at her quarterly review, keeping the direction
Keep the goal unchanged to show commitment to the original plan
quiz.x: The course says adjust goals when circumstances change without abandoning direction. Rewriting entirely is the runner-up but discards progress and the mission behind it.

quiz.q: Which capstone component most directly converts Kofi's 360 insights into behaviour change?
opts: A summary of his 360 themes included in the capstone document
Two high-leverage behaviours turned into SMART goals with actions
His refined leadership mission statement at the top of the plan
A list of his top three lids with the life-balance scores beside them
quiz.x: The Plan element turns 360 behaviours into SMART goals with milestones and weekly actions. The summary records insights but does not change behaviour.

facts.t: Average effect of implementation intentions on goal attainment in a 94-study meta-analysis.
facts.more: Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) found if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect. 'When X happens, I will do Y' beats good intentions.

facts.t: Year George Doran published the S.M.A.R.T. goals framework.
facts.more: Today usually read as Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Your plan needs three to five such goals, not ten.

facts.t: Team21's growth framework: Pray, Plan, People.
facts.more: Pray anchors you to values; Plan turns insight into SMART goals and if-then habits; People supply mentorship, accountability and observation.

facts.t: 'Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labour in vain.'
facts.more: A plan without an anchor tends to serve ambition rather than calling — the reason Pray comes first.
